This summer, I had the opportunity to work as an Automation Engineer Intern at OSF HealthCare, where I spent a lot of my time working with UiPath and learning how automation can be used in a real healthcare environment.

One of the projects I worked on involved automating the process of putting together presentations that were normally created by hand. The process required someone to find the correct files, organize the information, create the presentation, and send it to the people who needed it. I worked on building a UiPath automation that could handle a large part of that process automatically.

Throughout the project, I got experience working with UiPath Studio, Orchestrator, Apps, and different parts of the automation development process. I also spent a lot of time testing the workflow and fixing problems that came up when the automation had to deal with different files or unexpected situations.

One thing I learned from the project was how important it is to understand the process before trying to automate it. A process might look simple at first, but there can be a lot of smaller steps and exceptions that need to be considered.

Working on this project gave me a much better understanding of RPA and what goes into building an automation that someone can actually use. It was a great experience getting to apply what I have learned in school to a real project.

This summer I had the chance to work as an Automation Engineer Intern at OSF HealthCare where I spent quite a bit of time using UiPath and learning how automation is able to be used in healthcare.

One of the projects I was tasked with was automating how presentations were put together. Normally someone would have to go and find the right files, organize everything, make the presentation, and then send it to whoever needed it. I worked on developing a UiPath automation that could do a large part of this work for them.

Throughout making this project, I got to work with different parts of UiPath such as Studio, Orchestrator, and Apps. A good amount of my time went into trying different files and working through whatever problems came up with them. Some of those problems took more looking into than others, but doing this gave me more practice with testing, debugging, and understanding my own workflow as well.

I also learned how much there is to know about the way someone does their work before I can build something to do it for them. Something can seem pretty simple when someone explains it, but once you start working through it yourself there are smaller steps and exceptions that you have to account for as well.

All in all, this was a great project for me to learn more about RPA and what goes into making an automation that other people can actually use. I enjoyed getting to take what I've learned in school and use it on a real project at OSF!

Recently, I worked on a project comparing Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, with Context Augmented Generation to see how different ways of giving an LLM information can affect its answers.

For the project, I used a single document as the main source of information and tested different ways of getting that information into the model. With RAG, the document was split into smaller chunks and the system searched for the chunks that were most related to the question. With the other approach, more of the document was placed directly into the model's context.

I experimented with things such as chunk size and how many pieces of the document were retrieved for each question. I also had to think about the tradeoff between giving the model more information and using more context than was actually needed.

What interested me most was seeing how much the setup around the model can affect the final response. Using the same language model does not always mean getting the same quality of answer. The way information is stored, searched, and passed into the model can make a large difference.

This project gave me more experience working with LLMs, embeddings, vector search, and evaluating generated responses. It also helped me understand RAG beyond just knowing the definition and gave me a better idea of when it could actually be useful in a larger application.

Recently I worked on a project where I compared Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, with Context Augmented Generation to learn more about how the information given to an LLM can change the answers it gives.

For this project, I used one document as the source of information and tried different ways of giving that information to the model. With RAG, I split the document into smaller chunks that the system could search through to find what was relevant to the question. The other approach involved putting more of that text into the context from the start, so I wasn't relying on a search to pick out the parts for each question.

While working on the RAG version, I tried changing how much text went into each chunk and how many chunks were passed along to the model. This gave me different versions to compare when looking through the answers it generated. I also had to think about whether the extra text was useful for the question or if I was just filling up more of the context with information it didn't need.

The part I found most interesting was how much the setup around the model matters. Even when using the same model, the answers can be different depending on how you find the information and pass it in. This gave me more to think about besides which model I was using.

Throughout making this project, I got more experience with LLMs and the tools that go along with them such as embeddings, vector search, and evaluating responses. I now have a better understanding of how RAG works from actually using it, and where I could use it in future projects!

I recently finished working on a software project that used computer vision to help keep track of available parking spaces in a parking lot.

The idea behind the project was to take images from a camera and determine whether each parking space was empty or occupied. Instead of having someone manually keep track of available spaces, the program could process the image and update the number automatically.

I started by defining the different parking areas in the image and then worked on detecting whether a vehicle was inside each one. One of the harder parts was dealing with changes in lighting, shadows, and vehicles that did not always park in exactly the same position. Something that worked well on one image did not always work as well on another, so I had to test the program using different conditions.

I also created a simple interface that displayed the total number of open spaces and updated as new images were processed. This made it easier to see how the detection was performing instead of only looking at the output from the code.

This project gave me a chance to work with Python and computer vision while also dealing with a problem that could have a practical use. It showed me how much testing matters when software has to work with information coming from the real world instead of clean data that always looks the same.

One of the projects I recently worked on was a program for counting open parking spaces using images of a parking lot. For this project, I got to use Python and learn more about computer vision by working on how the program could tell whether a car was parked in a certain space.

The idea was to use images from a camera to figure out which spaces had cars in them and which ones were empty. Instead of someone having to count the spaces themselves, the program would go through the image and update the number for them.

To get started, I had to mark where each parking space was in the image so the program knew which areas to check for cars. From there, I worked on detecting whether those spaces were occupied. There were definitely a few things that made this more difficult, especially when the lighting changed or a shadow covered part of a spot. The cars weren't always parked in the same position either. I could get it working on one image but then have problems with another, which meant there was quite a bit of testing involved.

I also made a simple interface where someone could see the number of open spaces as new images were processed. Having the count displayed there gave me a way to check the results as it ran without needing to look through the code's output each time.

The testing ended up being a big part of what I learned, especially with how different the images could be even though they were showing the same parking areas. I had to keep checking it with different conditions and figure out what was causing it to miss things. Working through that gave me more experience with both Python and the problems that come with using actual camera images.

I recently had the opportunity to work on an automation project that gave me a much better understanding of how technology can be used to improve everyday processes.

The project focused on finding a task that normally takes a lot of manual work and building a way to make it faster and more consistent. While working on it, I was able to get more experience with automation tools, testing, debugging, and thinking through how a process should work from start to finish.

One of the biggest things I learned was that getting the automation to work is only part of the job. It also has to be easy for other people to use, understand, and maintain. I spent a lot of time fixing smaller issues, testing different cases, and making changes based on feedback.

There were definitely parts of the project that took longer than I expected, but that ended up being one of the most useful parts of the experience. Every issue forced me to slow down, figure out what was actually causing the problem, and find a better solution.

Overall, this project helped me improve both my technical skills and the way I approach problems. I am looking forward to continuing to learn more about automation and software development and using what I learned on future projects.
